title: Status epilepticus caused by cerebral amyloid angiopathy-related inflammation
case_prompt:
A 52-year-old man with a history of hypertension and alcohol abuse presented with two days of new-onset irritability, paranoia, and confusion. Forty-five minutes before admission, he experienced bright colors and stars in his right visual field followed by expressive aphasia; he could understand speech and formulate answers internally but was unable to speak. At an outside hospital, he had a witnessed seizure with leftward head deviation evolving into a generalized tonic–clonic seizure lasting 40 seconds, accompanied by tongue biting and postictal confusion without incontinence. On examination, he had a right inferior homonymous quadrant visual field defect, more pronounced in the right eye. 

A lumbar puncture revealed acellular cerebrospinal fluid with normal protein and glucose, no oligoclonal bands, and negative cytology and flow cytometry. Routine electroencephalography showed spike–wave discharges and several electrographic seizures in the left occipital region. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain demonstrated left occipital white matter and cortical T2 hyperintensity with mild focal mass effect, no enhancement, and petechial hemorrhages on gradient-echo sequences, as well as a smaller focus of T2 hyperintensity in the left anterior insula. Magnetic resonance angiography of the head and neck was unremarkable.

He was loaded with levetiracetam and discharged. The initial impression was multifocal glioma, less likely an infectious or inflammatory process, and even less likely an old stroke. After recurrent visual symptoms and aphasia, levetiracetam was increased, and a biopsy of the left occipital lesion was scheduled. 

A repeat MRI two months later showed significant improvement of the left occipital and insular lesions, leading to consideration of acute disseminated encephalomyelitis. The planned biopsy was aborted, and an inflammatory workup was undertaken. Repeat cerebrospinal fluid studies remained unrevealing. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis identified hepatic hemangiomas. Spinal MRI and CT angiography of the head and neck were unremarkable. He was discharged.

Follow-up MRI four months after presentation showed worsening left occipital T2 hyperintensity, new left frontal T2 hyperintensities, and new enhancement of a right anterior temporal lesion. A biopsy of the left occipital lesion was then performed.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Multifocal glioma — “the patient's history, exam, and studies were thought to be most consistent with a multifocal glioma”  
2. Infectious or inflammatory process — “less likely an infectious or inflammatory process”  
3. Old stroke — “even less likely an old stroke”  
4. Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM) — “These shifting lesions were thought to be more consistent with a demyelinating process such as acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM).”  
5. Seizure-related changes on PET — “These areas of increased FDG uptake were thought to be most likely due to an inflammatory process and less likely due to recent seizure activity.”
